claims.text: Accelerated coupled degradation is driven by synergy between mechanically induced surface roughening and preferential corrosion of specific phases.
The wear-corrosion interaction creates localized stress concentrations that accelerate material removal.
The initial alloy has a uniform multiphase eutectic microstructure with no pre-existing surface damage.
The controlled comparison comprises simultaneous wear-corrosion, wear-only, and corrosion-only exposures.
The relevant elevated-temperature range is approximately 500–800 °C.
Mechanical wear induces surface roughness.
Wear-induced roughening exposes phase boundaries.
Wear-induced surface features create stress concentrations.
Exposed phase boundaries corrode preferentially because the phases have different electrochemical potentials.
Preferential corrosion weakens the material and increases its susceptibility to wear.
Wear-induced exposure of fresh surfaces increases the corrosion rate.
The feedback between wear and preferential corrosion accelerates overall degradation.
Total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion will be significantly greater than the sum of degradation under wear-only and corrosion-only conditions.
The wear rate under simultaneous exposure will exceed the wear-only rate because corrosion weakens the material.
The corrosion rate under simultaneous exposure will exceed the corrosion-only rate because wear exposes fresh surfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies when constituent phases differ significantly in electrochemical potential and mechanical properties.
Elevated temperature enhances corrosion kinetics in the stated regime.
The strength of the synergistic interaction may depend on alloy composition and environmental conditions.
Failure to observe total simultaneous degradation significantly above the additive wear-only and corrosion-only losses would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe enhanced phase-specific corrosion at wear tracks would falsify the proposed localized mechanism.
